topic.title: Manipur Gets Elected Government After President's Rule

subtopics.title: New Government in Manipur
subtopics.summary: President Droupadi Murmu revoked President's Rule in Manipur after nearly one year, clearing the path for an elected government. Yumnam Khemchand Singh (BJP) was sworn in as the 13th Manipur Chief Minister. Two Deputy Chief Ministers, Nemcha Kipgen and Losii Dikho, took oath alongside him.

subtopics.title: Kuki-Zomi and Meitei Violence
subtopics.summary: Violence erupted between Kuki-Zomi tribals and the Meitei community, the first clash of its kind in three decades in Manipur. A key trigger was the Meitei demand for Scheduled Tribe (ST) status, which has persisted since 2012. A 2023 High Court direction to consider that request added to tensions with Kuki groups.

subtopics.title: Historical Background and Divides
subtopics.summary: Meiteis make up 52 per cent of Manipur's population and live mainly in valley areas covering about 10 per cent of the state. Hill areas cover 89 per cent of the land but have only 20 of the 60 assembly seats, while Meiteis hold 40. Meiteis are restricted from buying land in about 90 per cent of Manipur, whereas tribals can buy land in the Imphal Valley.

subtopics.title: President's Rule: Articles, Duration and Revocation
subtopics.summary: President's Rule is the Centre's takeover of a state government when the constitutional machinery fails, also called State Emergency. A proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within 2 months, and then continues for 6 months. It can be extended by Parliament up to a maximum of 3 years and can be revoked by the President at any time.

subtopics.title: Key Records and Judicial Review
subtopics.summary: Manipur has had President's Rule the most number of times, 11, followed by UP, J&K and Punjab. The first three instances were in Punjab, PEPSU and Andhra. In S.R. Bommai vs Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that the President's power to dismiss a state government is not absolute.

quizzes.title: New Government Check
quizzes.passage: Manipur has moved back to an elected government after nearly one year of direct central control. The state's administration was run by the Centre because the state government could not control a crisis in which violence broke out between Kuki-Zomi tribal groups and the Meitei community. Reports described it as the first clash of this kind in three decades in the state. The President revoked the arrangement, clearing the way for an elected government to take office. The new chief minister belongs to the Bharatiya Janata Party. Two deputy chief ministers were also sworn in, one from the Kuki-Zo community and one from the Naga community. Their presence reflects the state's mix of communities, which has long shaped its politics. The oath-taking marked the start of a new government after a long period without one. The roots of the conflict go back much further. The Meitei community lives mainly in the valley, which covers a small share of the state's land, while the hill areas cover most of it. Land purchase rules differ between the two regions. Disputes over census figures, the delimitation process and demands for tribal status have added to the tension between communities. The Meitei community has also raised concerns about inaccurate census figures from 2020. Critics have raised allegations of human rights abuses in affected regions, where the armed forces have extensive powers. Demands for autonomy from Nagas and Kukis have also been part of the state's politics for years.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about President's Rule in India:
I. Under Article 356, President's Rule can be imposed when the constitutional machinery of a state fails.
II. A proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within 2 months of its issue.
III. The President needs Parliament's approval to revoke a proclamation of President's Rule.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation: Statements I and II are correct, while III is wrong because a proclamation can be revoked by the President without Parliamentary approval.

questions.q:
How many of the following statements about President's Rule are correct?
I. A resolution approving the proclamation needs a simple majority in either House.
II. The President needs Parliament's approval to revoke a proclamation.
III. President's Rule can be extended up to a maximum period of 3 years with Parliament's approval.
IV. Jammu and Kashmir had the shortest single period under President's Rule.
questions.explanation: Statements I and III are correct, while II is wrong (no approval is needed for revocation) and IV is wrong (J&K had the longest single period).

questions.q: Which state has experienced President's Rule the most number of times?
questions.explanation: Manipur has had President's Rule 11 times, the most of any state listed in the booklet.

quizzes.title: President's Rule Recall
quizzes.passage: President's Rule is the term used when the Centre takes over the government of a state. The Constitution gives the Centre a duty to make sure that every state government is carried on in accordance with its provisions. When a state's constitutional machinery fails, the Centre can take over under a separate Article, which lets the President issue a proclamation if satisfied that a state government cannot function as the Constitution requires. Such a proclamation is also used when a state does not comply with directions from the Centre. Once a proclamation is issued, Parliament must approve it within a fixed time. If both Houses approve, the arrangement continues for a fixed period. It can be extended, but only with Parliament's approval and only up to an overall limit. During this time, the President can take over the functions of the state government and the powers of the Governor or other executive authorities. The President can also declare that the powers of the state legislature will be exercised by Parliament. A proclamation can be revoked by the President at any time through a later proclamation, and such a revocation does not need Parliamentary approval. Resolutions approving the proclamation in either House need only a simple majority of members present and voting. These rules on duration, approval and revocation are the main points to remember for this topic.
